assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: R-group
items.clue: The variable side chain of an amino acid.

items.label: Polypeptide
items.clue: A chain of many amino acids linked by peptide bonds.

items.label: Essential amino acid
items.clue: Cannot be made in the body, so it must come from food.

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by all 20 of the amino acids that are coded for in the genetic code?

options.text: An amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and an R-group are all bonded to one alpha carbon atom.
The R-group is identical in every amino acid, and the amine and carboxyl groups are what vary.
The amine group is bonded directly to the carbon atom of the carboxyl group, with no carbon between.
The amine group is an NH₃ group, with the same structure as a molecule of ammonia.

questions.stem: Two amino acids react to form a dipeptide. Which statement describes this reaction?

options.text: A molecule of water is taken in to provide the atoms needed to link the two amino acids together.
The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amine group of the other, and water is released.
The R-group of one amino acid bonds to the R-group of the other, forming the peptide bond between them.
The amine group of one amino acid forms a hydrogen bond with the carboxyl group of the other, and no water is released.

questions.stem: What is meant by an essential amino acid?

options.text: One that the body needs in larger quantities than the non-essential amino acids.
One of the 20 amino acids, all of which must be supplied by the protein in the diet.
One that is found in animal protein but is absent from all plant-based foods.
One that cannot be synthesized in the body and must be obtained from food.

questions.explanation: This is the definition: essential amino acids cannot be synthesized and must be obtained from food, whereas non-essential amino acids can be made from other amino acids.

questions.stem: A chemist makes tripeptides using only four different amino acids. Each of the three positions in a chain can hold any of the four amino acids. How many different tripeptides are possible?
When egg white is heated, its soluble proteins turn into a white solid. What has happened to the protein molecules?

options.text: Heat has broken the peptide bonds, so the polypeptides have been split into amino acids.
Heat has killed the proteins, so they are no longer able to carry out their functions.
Heat has changed their shape temporarily, and they will refold as soon as the egg white cools.
Heat has broken the bonds holding their folded shape, so they have unfolded.

questions.stem: A polypeptide of 150 amino acids is assembled by condensation reactions. How does the number of water molecules change as the whole chain is formed?

options.text: 150 released
300 released
149 released
149 consumed

questions.explanation: Each condensation reaction links two amino acids with one peptide bond and releases one molecule of water. Joining 150 amino acids into one chain needs 149 peptide bonds, so 149 water molecules are released.

questions.stem: Why is the number of different possible polypeptides described as effectively infinite?

options.text: The 20 amino acids can be arranged in any order, but each amino acid can be used only once in a given chain.
There are very many combinations of amino acids, and the order of the amino acids does not affect the protein.
Chains can be of any length, and the 20 amino acids can occur in any order and be used any number of times.
Each extra amino acid added to a chain adds 20 to the number of different polypeptides that are possible.

questions.stem: Which statement about the R-groups of amino acids is correct?

options.text: Every hydrophilic R-group must carry a charge; a polar R-group that is uncharged is classed as hydrophobic.
Hydrophilic R-groups are either polar but uncharged, or charged, and charged R-groups are acidic or basic.
An acidic R-group carries a positive charge, because an acid is a substance that contains hydrogen ions.
R-groups have little effect on a polypeptide, whose properties come from its amine and carboxyl groups.

questions.stem: What stabilizes the alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets of a protein's secondary structure?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between the R-groups of amino acids brought close together by folding.
Disulfide bonds between cysteines spaced at regular intervals along the polypeptide.
Hydrogen bonds forming the peptide links between the amine and carboxyl groups of neighbours.
Hydrogen bonds at regular positions between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares insulin, collagen and haemoglobin?

options.text: All three are conjugated proteins, because each of them is built from more than one polypeptide chain.
The haem groups of haemoglobin are short polypeptides, so all three of these proteins are non-conjugated.
Insulin is a single polypeptide, so unlike collagen and haemoglobin it does not have quaternary structure.
Haemoglobin is a conjugated protein with haem groups; insulin and collagen are non-conjugated.
